quote: but that there was a corresponding old Persian legend about the Babylonian gods Marduk and Ishtar, and the rival Elamite gods Humman and Vashti
content: The Persian legend of a divine conflict is Jensen's 1892 conjecture, not archaeology, and the sentence overstates it. That concession stands. The etymology survived, though. Mordecai is a Babylonian theophoric name built on Marduk, and a Persian official called Marduka is attested in the Persepolis Fortification tablets. The Esther–Ishtar link remains a standard, if debated, derivation. Scholars kept the names and dropped the myth-conflict. The woman's evidence was half outdated and half sound, and the essay's point does not depend on it. That point is that she held the historical case against Esther, with the silence of the Persian records that Fable calls "the actual argument," alongside her observance.

quote: She hasn’t actually deceived herself into believing that God exists or that the Jewish religion is true. Not even close, so far as I can tell.
content: Van Leeuwen's framework supports the essay's diagnosis. He argues that religious credence is a different attitude from factual belief, with different inputs and a different role in behaviour (Van Leeuwen 2014). What the woman told the author was that she had been an atheist in high school, acted as if she believed, and "over time, she came to really believe in God." That is a claim to have acquired factual belief. If what she acquired was credence, as every observation suggests and as Fable agrees, then her report about her own attitude is wrong in exactly the way the essay says: she believes she has deceived herself into belief, and she has not. The essay supplied the lay version of Van Leeuwen's distinction, and his framework makes her self-report the anomaly.
